PEMBURY - NOT SUCH A HAPPY LIFESTYLE

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
False promises from a listed company running a group of private schools and retirement homes

Unique Selling Point:
Angry people - insiders prepared to go on the record. Lots of documents to prove the case and revealing new facts not known up until now - a Carte Blanche exclusive investigation

Summary:
A listed JSE company called Pembury Lifestyle group say they are offering affordable, quality private school education and they have big expansion plans. But while the CEO and his directors take home considerable salaries, parents, teachers and a former headmaster go on the record to say PLG breaks its promises, skimps on basics and doesn’t give a damn about the quality of education its providing.


Further information:
In March 2017 Andrew McLouchlan, the CEO and majority shareholder listed the Pembury lifestyle group on the JSE ALTX. They had big plans and began buying up properties and opening schools. They also say the group would explore the potential acquisition of retirement accommodation and services, and currently there are 4 or five retirement lodges. But only two years later, the group is in trouble and the future of old people and hundreds of young kids hang in the balance. Only they don’t know, because PLG head office is trying to keep things under the radar.

At the last minute in April, the group posted their consolidated audited summarized financials. But the financials appear to be written by a schizophrenic accountant. On the first few pages PLG talks about expansion and profitability at the schools. But by page four they have given up any attempt at pretence and warn that there are serious concerns about PLG as a going concern. Its clear the company is deep in debt and Carte Blanche has uncovered that they are defaulting on at least 50% of the schools they have purchased. Today the Springs school has, after 3 years of fighting sent them a notice cancelling the deal. And they are not alone. Across Gauteng this week, lawyers are meeting to find a way to hold PLG to account.

Now to the schools who are holding open days to attract new children as disenchanted parents remove their kids from the schools.

“ To get an increase and a netball pitch we need to get 125 learners” says one teacher off the record, but our numbers are down to 55.”

She calls the education a joke and lists a litany of problems with what is happening at school- from unqualified teachers to no money for pens, its an uphill struggle.
While the local government school charges around R600 per month, PLG can charge up to R5000 per month depending on the grade.

“There are better facilities at the government school” she says.

And don’t get the parents started. They have complained about lack of teaching, lack of facilities, one school operating illegally, no PTA, no decent security for the schools and an endless array of broken promises. Many parents have removed their children from the schools and some have had to repeat grades. “It’s a complete shambles’ says one mother.

Pembury boasts that they have an 87% matric pass rate, but that is based on one school whose only written once. Now a second group is about to face one of the most important tests of their lives and their former headmaster is beside himself with concern. He was ousted when he went along to the auction of his own school property. PLG dismissed him saying he shouldn’t have been there, he abandoned his post, even though it was school holidays.

And now it seems according to one lawyer that Pembury has a particular modus operandi. He says they are beyond dodgy and their M.O appears to be to buy properties, agree to pay an amount and then default on the balance and the occupational rent. That is what happened to the Sandton retirement lodge and when they left, he alleges they stripped the place bare and even took the taps.

Carte Blanche can reveal that PLG has defaulted on at least four of the properties, which means at any time the schools can find they have nowhere to go and must close down. We ask some tough questions of Andrew McLoughlan and his directors who hold the future of many children in their hands.

Press Release:


School Yard Blues
It’s a company that listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange in 2017 amid grand promises of affordable private school education. But the dream that the company sold came crashing down for some parents and their children, when they realized that the promises didn’t materialize for them. With the company’s own auditors sounding warnings in their financials, Carte Blanche lifts the corporate veil, analyzing the numbers and speaking to former teachers, headmasters and disillusioned parents.
Producer: Joy Summers
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender
Researcher: Tony Beamish


Script:


PLG FINAL SCRIPT TX SUNDAY 16th JUNE 2019 SCHOOL YARD BLUES

Commentary One
In 2018 Louise Barney was excited that a new private school in Randfontein would open its doors and pave the way for her daughter’s future

Louise Barney
When we heard Randfontein was getting a private school, it was for many, many parents, a great option, and we all flooded, we ran! She laughs

Commentary Two
The school was PLG Green Hills. Its one of eleven private schools in the Pembury Lifestyle group stable. Fees range between R23 000 to R58 000 rand annually, so these schools marketed as affordable quality education, are sought after. But within a month Louise started questioning what she was paying for

Louise
my very first problem was half of the staff component was still student teachers.

Commentary three
She wasn’t the only parent with concerns, Sharon Thomas and Dolores Arnolds dreams of a better education for their daughters, also soon evaporated

Sharon
We got to the school the grass was uncut, it was gravel. It was shocking when we got there basically! And we thought this is not what we were promised, there were going to be tennis courts, sports fields…
Doloros
A swimming Pool
Sharon
A swimming pool..

Commentary Four
Pembury say Green Hills has a peaceful country setting. Our footage confirmed what the parents were saying. Sports fields and decent play areas for the children aren’t there. Inside, the school resembles a mortuary, there are small windows, and there were often problems with electricity which they buy from the next- door neighbor.

Louis
They had electricity problems, and because there was no electricity it was very dark in that classroom, and very poor ventilation in the classrooms, so what happened they had to sit on the floor in foyer to do their work

Commentary Five
After a month she asked to see her daughter’s books

Louise
It was actually very scary, there was some books that had the cover page where they started drawing- and that was a month into the first term.

Commentary Six
Louise removed her daughter after the first term, but Sharon and Dolores couldn’t afford to remove their children from the school.

Doloros
You have no idea what it takes for a parent like myself who is a single parent trying to give their children the best that they can, and that is what is hurting me the most, that my daughter is suffering because of their greed

Commentary Seven
Then what they discovered at a meeting, shocked them, and set these feisty mothers on a collision course with PLG

Sharon
One of the ex- teachers that was there said: “you have a problem with the children not getting homework, your REAL problem should be for the fact that the school is not registered!” So I turned to the principle and said what do you mean?

Commentary eight
They soon realised the teacher had been right. PLG was running the school illegally.
DEVI
What did you find out?
Sharon
The Randfontein district don’t even know who PLG was.

Commentary nine
Then the Gauteng department confirmed in this letter that the school was operating illegally. That was January, so what’s happened since? Last month we asked the same question, when we went in posing undercover as prospective parents

Riaan
Is this place registered?
Teacher
No, we are in the process of registration, but it’s not finalized yet

DEVI LINK
During our research we have spoken to former and current headmasters, added to that, teachers and parents. A few are satisfied, but many, many others are deeply unhappy.

Commentary ten
At Pembury’s Hartbeespoort campus, the kids look happy, but some parents aren’t, and the principal has just resigned. These minutes from February record their unhappiness:

• Teachers get low salaries and are resigning
• The quality of education is in question
• Parents worry about the safety of the building structures
• They ask why there are still containers after so many years.
• Internet, computer lab and Wi-Fi is an issue
• Kids aren’t served proper food
• and parents are concerned their children could get abducted because of lax security


Commentary Ten A
PLG claim that they have fixed the problems and the parents are now happy. But these troubles are familiar for the former headmaster at PLG’s Mellow Oaks school

Andrew Stewart
for me it’s a company that just neglects, abuses. I would suggest that there is huge level of ineptitude and incompetence, but the driving factor as far as I can see it is greed.

Commentary Eleven
When he took up his post he was shocked at the state of the school

Andrew
You could see it hadn’t been maintained, there were garden lamps lying flat on their sides, their wires exposed, going into the staff room, it’s a rondavel, not a window in sight, so it’s just a space and every single light bulb had blown, and later on when I asked for light bulbs I simply got no response to any requests for maintenance

Commentary twelve
Almost four years since inception, there are still 13 container classrooms, the swimming pool hasn’t materialized, his teachers lacked text books and projectors, and with no Umalusi accreditation yet, he is worried about the current matrics. PLG says the schools are fully funded. The financials say the schools are profitable. Last year they earned R82 million in revenue.

Devi
How much were you given to run the school per month
Andrew
I wasn’t given anything to run the school. The money comes in from parents and goes directly to PLG head office, so the school itself has no budget
Devi
So how were you supposed to run the school then?
Andrew Stewart
Begging and pleading

Commentary thirteen
And by the end of last year Sharon and Dolores had had enough and removed their daughters

Sharon
I feel robbed. I feel that we were undermined by the PLG group, because they sold us a pipe dream that we never received, and the biggest injustice is to our children who were at the school as well.

In a written reply which we have summarized, Pembury say

Pembury lifestyle group is proud of the level of quality of the schools. In Randfontein the school is on its fourth principal, there are currently 4 student teachers. We have submitted our application for a license. Electricity and water is procured from the neighbors. Maintenance at our schools is of paramount importance (lightbulb)

Commentary fourteen
In March 2017 Pembury Lifestyle group listed on the JSE ALT X. Meet the boss and majority shareholder Andrew McLachlan.
Drum Roll
No wonder his directors are smiling. The listing raised R140 million rand in cash for the company

PLG say the money was primarily used to buy the properties that PLG schools occupy, but Carte Blanche has established that they have only paid a fraction of the purchase prices for the schools, and now the group is running on empty

LINK
Perhaps the best indication of how the directors are managing Pembury is the share price. Listed at a R1, its now sitting at only 10 cents a share. And even their own auditors are cautioning investors.

Commentary fifteen
PLG say the company is in a sound financial position, but the auditors are worried about its future. Andre Prakke is a leading forensic auditor

Andre Prakke
What it amounts to is for the next 12 months they are not sure that the company will generate enough cash to survive.

Commentary Sixteen
And that could leave almost 3000 children and the residents of their retirement lodges stranded. So, what’s going on at this listed company? For three weeks we’ve been asking. Last Monday we went to their offices.

Devi: The cars are here, the people are here, but the lights don’t seem to be on. There is There is no way we are going to get answers today.

Commentary Seventeen
Pembury later sent their responses through their lawyer Paul Barnard. They say that they have been transparent, but as we dug deeper, we found that Pembury was not honouring its debts

Andrew
On the 7th March this year, I was shocked to find the sheriff and he was standing there with a notice of execution telling me that the school was going to be auctioned.

Commentary eighteen
Our sources claim that PLG buys up properties, pay a small deposit, and then defaults on the purchase price, while still earning millions from the school fees. That’s what happened at Mellow Oaks. They bought the property for R12 million, paid only R500 000 deposit and then defaulted. So the owner attached the school and put it on auction, and that is where the former headmaster bumped into company COO Sheldon Neilson

Andrew
When I walked in there Mr. Sheldon Neilson was standing in the room but instead of talking to me he phoned me and said please don’t acknowledge his presence or to show that I recognized him.
Devi
Why?
I didn’t know at the time but I could only assume something underhand was going on

Commentary nineteen
What he later discovered was that the COO was bidding for the property under the name of a corporation owned by one of Pembury’s directors. They hoped to get the property they had defaulted on, at half the price they had originally agreed to. Soon after Andrew Stewart was fired for deserting his post and breach of trust. He has gone to the CCMA for unfair dismissal

Andrew
The charges were, I had deserted my post by attending the auction
Devi
But it’s the school holidays
Andrew
It’s the school holidays and I am the headmaster of the school and I need to manage risk

Commentary twenty
PLG say they disclosed the circumstances of the auction, they are trying to recover the school through legal processes and that they will protect the school and staff to the full extent of the law

But how can they protect schools if they default on the properties? And now lawyers are demanding they pay up.

Here at Willow View Academy, R10 million is outstanding on areas rental and the owners have cancelled the agreement. Pembury say they own the school, but transfer has been delayed

WHOOSH

It’s the same story at PLG NORTH RIDING

WHOOSH
At PLG Midview R14 million is outstanding.

WHOOSH.

At their Allan’s view campus they have only paid R500 000 of a R7.5 million debt.

WHOOSH

PLG say there is no dispute over these schools, and they are negotiating extensions. The Centurion School is one of the few that is fully paid up, but it took the owner Christelle Van Rooyen, 18 months to get her money. PLG says she was compensated for the delay.

Christelle Van Rooyen
Oh it was a big struggle, it was a nightmare dealing with these people, really. They didn’t adhere to any conditions, they just didn’t honour any contracts for that matter

Commentary Twenty- one
PLG assures Carte Blanche that all their rentals are up to date. But
less than 30% of the properties they claim as their own, are paid for. At the Melrose Arch retirement lodge, also in default, they sold life rights to residents without the owner’s permission or knowledge. PLG say they complied substantially with the legislation

Devi
This sounds like a mess?
Andre
It is a mess, and somewhere bubble will burst

Commentary Twenty- two
That may be sooner rather than later, because a small company that was not paid for these sports courts has applied to the high court to liquidate the group. PLG say they are in the process of resolving the matter. On Thursday the group announced it was walking away from its retirement lodge business.

THE END 12 06

PROMO ONE
A JSE listed company say they offer affordable private school education, but a former headmaster tells Carte Blanche how he had to beg and plead for money just to get the basics for his school





PROMO TWO
A JSE listed company offering private school education, raised money to buy the properties that housed their schools. Two years later they’re embroiled in legal disputes and are running on empty

PROMO THREE
Are parents getting what they were promised at a listed company that offers private school education
Sharon
I feel that we were undermined, because they sold us a pipe dream that we never received



NAMES

LOUISE BARNEY
SHARON THOMAS
DOLORES ARNOLDS
ANDREW STEWART FORMER HEADMASTER MELLOW OAKS
ANDRE PRAKKE FORENSIC AUDITOR
CHRISTELLE VAN ROOYEN

Producer: Joy Summers Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender Researcher: Tony Beamish Script: PLG FINAL SCRIPT TX SUNDAY 16th JUNE 2019 SCHOOL YARD BLUES Commentary One In 2018 Louise Barney was excited that a new private school in Randfontein would open its doors and pave the way for her daughter’s future Louise Barney When we heard Randfontein was getting a private school, it was for many, many parents, a great option, and we all flooded, we ran! She laughs Commentary Two The school was PLG Green Hills. Its one of eleven private schools in the Pembury Lifestyle group stable. Fees range between R23 000 to R58 000 rand annually, so these schools marketed as affordable quality education, are sought after. But within a month Louise started questioning what she was paying for Louise my very first problem was half of the staff component was still student teachers. Commentary three She wasn’t the only parent with concerns, Sharon Thomas and Dolores Arnolds dreams of a better education for their daughters, also soon evaporated Sharon We got to the school the grass was uncut, it was gravel. It was shocking when we got there basically! And we thought this is not what we were promised, there were going to be tennis courts, sports fields… Doloros A swimming Pool Sharon A swimming pool.. Commentary Four Pembury say Green Hills has a peaceful country setting. Our footage confirmed what the parents were saying. Sports fields and decent play areas for the children aren’t there. Inside, the school resembles a mortuary, there are small windows, and there were often problems with electricity which they buy from the next- door neighbor. Louis They had electricity problems, and because there was no electricity it was very dark in that classroom, and very poor ventilation in the classrooms, so what happened they had to sit on the floor in foyer to do their work Commentary Five After a month she asked to see her daughter’s books Louise It was actually very scary, there was some books that had the cover page where they started drawing- and that was a month into the first term. Commentary Six Louise removed her daughter after the first term, but Sharon and Dolores couldn’t afford to remove their children from the school. Doloros You have no idea what it takes for a parent like myself who is a single parent trying to give their children the best that they can, and that is what is hurting me the most, that my daughter is suffering because of their greed Commentary Seven Then what they discovered at a meeting, shocked them, and set these feisty mothers on a collision course with PLG Sharon One of the ex- teachers that was there said: “you have a problem with the children not getting homework, your REAL problem should be for the fact that the school is not registered!” So I turned to the principle and said what do you mean? Commentary eight They soon realised the teacher had been right. PLG was running the school illegally. DEVI What did you find out? Sharon The Randfontein district don’t even know who PLG was. Commentary nine Then the Gauteng department confirmed in this letter that the school was operating illegally. That was January, so what’s happened since? Last month we asked the same question, when we went in posing undercover as prospective parents Riaan Is this place registered? Teacher No, we are in the process of registration, but it’s not finalized yet DEVI LINK During our research we have spoken to former and current headmasters, added to that, teachers and parents. A few are satisfied, but many, many others are deeply unhappy. Commentary ten At Pembury’s Hartbeespoort campus, the kids look happy, but some parents aren’t, and the principal has just resigned. These minutes from February record their unhappiness: • Teachers get low salaries and are resigning • The quality of education is in question • Parents worry about the safety of the building structures • They ask why there are still containers after so many years. • Internet, computer lab and Wi-Fi is an issue • Kids aren’t served proper food • and parents are concerned their children could get abducted because of lax security Commentary Ten A PLG claim that they have fixed the problems and the parents are now happy. But these troubles are familiar for the former headmaster at PLG’s Mellow Oaks school Andrew Stewart for me it’s a company that just neglects, abuses. I would suggest that there is huge level of ineptitude and incompetence, but the driving factor as far as I can see it is greed. Commentary Eleven When he took up his post he was shocked at the state of the school Andrew You could see it hadn’t been maintained, there were garden lamps lying flat on their sides, their wires exposed, going into the staff room, it’s a rondavel, not a window in sight, so it’s just a space and every single light bulb had blown, and later on when I asked for light bulbs I simply got no response to any requests for maintenance Commentary twelve Almost four years since inception, there are still 13 container classrooms, the swimming pool hasn’t materialized, his teachers lacked text books and projectors, and with no Umalusi accreditation yet, he is worried about the current matrics. PLG says the schools are fully funded. The financials say the schools are profitable. Last year they earned R82 million in revenue. Devi How much were you given to run the school per month Andrew I wasn’t given anything to run the school. The money comes in from parents and goes directly to PLG head office, so the school itself has no budget Devi So how were you supposed to run the school then? Andrew Stewart Begging and pleading Commentary thirteen And by the end of last year Sharon and Dolores had had enough and removed their daughters Sharon I feel robbed. I feel that we were undermined by the PLG group, because they sold us a pipe dream that we never received, and the biggest injustice is to our children who were at the school as well. In a written reply which we have summarized, Pembury say Pembury lifestyle group is proud of the level of quality of the schools. In Randfontein the school is on its fourth principal, there are currently 4 student teachers. We have submitted our application for a license. Electricity and water is procured from the neighbors. Maintenance at our schools is of paramount importance (lightbulb) Commentary fourteen In March 2017 Pembury Lifestyle group listed on the JSE ALT X. Meet the boss and majority shareholder Andrew McLachlan. Drum Roll No wonder his directors are smiling. The listing raised R140 million rand in cash for the company PLG say the money was primarily used to buy the properties that PLG schools occupy, but Carte Blanche has established that they have only paid a fraction of the purchase prices for the schools, and now the group is running on empty LINK Perhaps the best indication of how the directors are managing Pembury is the share price. Listed at a R1, its now sitting at only 10 cents a share. And even their own auditors are cautioning investors. Commentary fifteen PLG say the company is in a sound financial position, but the auditors are worried about its future. Andre Prakke is a leading forensic auditor Andre Prakke What it amounts to is for the next 12 months they are not sure that the company will generate enough cash to survive. Commentary Sixteen And that could leave almost 3000 children and the residents of their retirement lodges stranded. So, what’s going on at this listed company? For three weeks we’ve been asking. Last Monday we went to their offices. Devi: The cars are here, the people are here, but the lights don’t seem to be on. There is There is no way we are going to get answers today. Commentary Seventeen Pembury later sent their responses through their lawyer Paul Barnard. They say that they have been transparent, but as we dug deeper, we found that Pembury was not honouring its debts Andrew On the 7th March this year, I was shocked to find the sheriff and he was standing there with a notice of execution telling me that the school was going to be auctioned. Commentary eighteen Our sources claim that PLG buys up properties, pay a small deposit, and then defaults on the purchase price, while still earning millions from the school fees. That’s what happened at Mellow Oaks. They bought the property for R12 million, paid only R500 000 deposit and then defaulted. So the owner attached the school and put it on auction, and that is where the former headmaster bumped into company COO Sheldon Neilson Andrew When I walked in there Mr. Sheldon Neilson was standing in the room but instead of talking to me he phoned me and said please don’t acknowledge his presence or to show that I recognized him. Devi Why? I didn’t know at the time but I could only assume something underhand was going on Commentary nineteen What he later discovered was that the COO was bidding for the property under the name of a corporation owned by one of Pembury’s directors. They hoped to get the property they had defaulted on, at half the price they had originally agreed to. Soon after Andrew Stewart was fired for deserting his post and breach of trust. He has gone to the CCMA for unfair dismissal Andrew The charges were, I had deserted my post by attending the auction Devi But it’s the school holidays Andrew It’s the school holidays and I am the headmaster of the school and I need to manage risk Commentary twenty PLG say they disclosed the circumstances of the auction, they are trying to recover the school through legal processes and that they will protect the school and staff to the full extent of the law But how can they protect schools if they default on the properties? And now lawyers are demanding they pay up. Here at Willow View Academy, R10 million is outstanding on areas rental and the owners have cancelled the agreement. Pembury say they own the school, but transfer has been delayed WHOOSH It’s the same story at PLG NORTH RIDING WHOOSH At PLG Midview R14 million is outstanding. WHOOSH. At their Allan’s view campus they have only paid R500 000 of a R7.5 million debt. WHOOSH PLG say there is no dispute over these schools, and they are negotiating extensions. The Centurion School is one of the few that is fully paid up, but it took the owner Christelle Van Rooyen, 18 months to get her money. PLG says she was compensated for the delay. Christelle Van Rooyen Oh it was a big struggle, it was a nightmare dealing with these people, really. They didn’t adhere to any conditions, they just didn’t honour any contracts for that matter Commentary Twenty- one PLG assures Carte Blanche that all their rentals are up to date. But less than 30% of the properties they claim as their own, are paid for. At the Melrose Arch retirement lodge, also in default, they sold life rights to residents without the owner’s permission or knowledge. PLG say they complied substantially with the legislation Devi This sounds like a mess? Andre It is a mess, and somewhere bubble will burst Commentary Twenty- two That may be sooner rather than later, because a small company that was not paid for these sports courts has applied to the high court to liquidate the group. PLG say they are in the process of resolving the matter. On Thursday the group announced it was walking away from its retirement lodge business. THE END 12 06 PROMO ONE A JSE listed company say they offer affordable private school education, but a former headmaster tells Carte Blanche how he had to beg and plead for money just to get the basics for his school PROMO TWO A JSE listed company offering private school education, raised money to buy the properties that housed their schools. Two years later they’re embroiled in legal disputes and are running on empty PROMO THREE Are parents getting what they were promised at a listed company that offers private school education Sharon I feel that we were undermined, because they sold us a pipe dream that we never received NAMES LOUISE BARNEY SHARON THOMAS DOLORES ARNOLDS ANDREW STEWART FORMER HEADMASTER MELLOW OAKS ANDRE PRAKKE FORENSIC AUDITOR CHRISTELLE VAN ROOYEN Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for PEMBURY - NOT SUCH A HAPPY LIFESTYLE (5454) Joy Summers 20 June 2019

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): False promises from a listed company running a group of private schools and retirement homes
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Angry people - insiders prepared to go on the record. Lots of documents to prove the case and revealing new facts not known up until now - a Carte Blanche exclusive investigation
metadata.Summary: A listed JSE company called Pembury Lifestyle group say they are offering affordable, quality private school education and they have big expansion plans. But while the CEO and his directors take home considerable salaries, parents, teachers and a former headmaster go on the record to say PLG breaks its promises, skimps on basics and doesn’t give a damn about the quality of education its providing.
metadata.Further information: In March 2017 Andrew McLouchlan, the CEO and majority shareholder listed the Pembury lifestyle group on the JSE ALTX. They had big plans and began buying up properties and opening schools. They also say the group would explore the potential acquisition of retirement accommodation and services, and currently there are 4 or five retirement lodges. But only two years later, the group is in trouble and the future of old people and hundreds of young kids hang in the balance. Only they don’t know, because PLG head office is trying to keep things under the radar. At the last minute in April, the group posted their consolidated audited summarized financials. But the financials appear to be written by a schizophrenic accountant. On the first few pages PLG talks about expansion and profitability at the schools. But by page four they have given up any attempt at pretence and warn that there are serious concerns about PLG as a going concern. Its clear the company is deep in debt and Carte Blanche has uncovered that they are defaulting on at least 50% of the schools they have purchased. Today the Springs school has, after 3 years of fighting sent them a notice cancelling the deal. And they are not alone. Across Gauteng this week, lawyers are meeting to find a way to hold PLG to account. Now to the schools who are holding open days to attract new children as disenchanted parents remove their kids from the schools. “ To get an increase and a netball pitch we need to get 125 learners” says one teacher off the record, but our numbers are down to 55.” She calls the education a joke and lists a litany of problems with what is happening at school- from unqualified teachers to no money for pens, its an uphill struggle. While the local government school charges around R600 per month, PLG can charge up to R5000 per month depending on the grade. “There are better facilities at the government school” she says. And don’t get the parents started. They have complained about lack of teaching, lack of facilities, one school operating illegally, no PTA, no decent security for the schools and an endless array of broken promises. Many parents have removed their children from the schools and some have had to repeat grades. “It’s a complete shambles’ says one mother. Pembury boasts that they have an 87% matric pass rate, but that is based on one school whose only written once. Now a second group is about to face one of the most important tests of their lives and their former headmaster is beside himself with concern. He was ousted when he went along to the auction of his own school property. PLG dismissed him saying he shouldn’t have been there, he abandoned his post, even though it was school holidays. And now it seems according to one lawyer that Pembury has a particular modus operandi. He says they are beyond dodgy and their M.O appears to be to buy properties, agree to pay an amount and then default on the balance and the occupational rent. That is what happened to the Sandton retirement lodge and when they left, he alleges they stripped the place bare and even took the taps. Carte Blanche can reveal that PLG has defaulted on at least four of the properties, which means at any time the schools can find they have nowhere to go and must close down. We ask some tough questions of Andrew McLoughlan and his directors who hold the future of many children in their hands.
